summary: HabWatch is a crew health dashboard for long-duration missions, focused on NASA’s “Hostile/Closed Environments” hazard. In a sealed habitat, the cabin itself shapes crew health: microbes spread more easily, stress can change the immune system, and temperature, noise, lighting and crowding all affect wellbeing. HabWatch puts cabin conditions (CO₂, O₂, pressure, temperature, humidity, noise, particles, water quality) on one screen with each crew member’s vitals, symptoms and saliva-based viral-shedding results. It then connects the two. For example, a CO₂ pocket at one sleep station is linked to that astronaut’s morning headache, and a feverish crew member’s shared surfaces appear on a contagion map. Every alert gives plain-language actions and says whether the crew can self-treat or should notify a flight surgeon. Because Mars missions face communication delays of up to about 20 minutes and a roughly two-week blackout during solar conjunction, HabWatch includes a blackout mode that turns every “notify ground” action into a step-by-step onboard plan. That way, astronauts can assess and act on their health on their own.
details:
What it does / how it works. HabWatch is a single-page dashboard for a 4-person Mars surface habitat, a scenario extrapolated from NASA's HERA analog (4 crew, 650 sq ft, 45-day simulated Mars missions with growing communication delays). It has:

  • A header with mission sol, Mars local time and Earth time, one-way ground delay, and overall crew status.
    1. CO₂ at each sleep station, linked to next-morning symptoms
    2. Latent-virus reactivation from saliva samples
    3. A crew contagion map of shared surfaces
    4. Water-system biofilm watch (biocide, organic carbon, culture status)
    5. Pharmacy expiry tracking, so alerts only suggest in-date medicine
    6. Circadian lighting mode and next switch
    7. Mars sol vs Earth clock and per-crew sleep drift
    8. Daily noise dose with earplug flags and hearing-test reminders
    9. Solar conjunction blackout mode
    10. Crowding: free space per person and a private-time log

Benefits and impact. Astronauts get one place that turns habitat data into decisions: what is wrong, who is affected, what to do, and whether the ground needs to know. That matters most on deep-space missions where help from Earth is delayed or unavailable.

Tools. HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in one self-contained file. There are no external libraries, server or install, and it runs offline in any browser. Simulated data drives the demo.

Creativity. Most health apps look only at the body. HabWatch treats the habitat as part of the patient and links environmental causes to physical effects. It also covers spaceflight-specific risks such as CO₂ pooling in microgravity, the longer Mars sol, and the conjunction blackout.

Factors considered. Fast reading for a busy crew, color coding, plain-language explanations (the crew are not all doctors), communication delay and loss of contact, medicine shelf life, privacy and stress in a small habitat, and offline reliability. Thresholds in the demo are illustrative and would be validated with flight surgeons before real use.
